"Let's go put your sweater on," Sage says.

contents.text: Authors don't always tell you everything. Sometimes, you need to make a guess about something in a story. Use what the story tells you and what you already know about life to make a good guess.
It can help to think about these questions:

elements.text: What is the character doing or saying?
Why might the character be acting that way?
What do I know about life that can help me figure this out?

contents.text: Let's look at an example:
Ben ran as fast as he could. He ran past Luke and Archer. "I won!" Ben shouted.
The author doesn't say what Ben is doing, but you can probably figure it out.
The character in this story is running. He runs past two people. Then he says, "I won!"
You probably know from real life that people usually do these things when they are running a race.
So, you can make a good guess that Ben is running a race.

contents.text: When you write, you can use sensory details. These sense words help your reader understand what something looks, sounds, tastes, smells, or feels like.

table.text: These are words like bright, clean, and purple. A reader can imagine looking at these details.
These are words like hissing, buzzing, and ringing. A reader can imagine hearing these details.
These are words like juicy, sweet, and burnt. A reader can imagine tasting these details.
These are words like fruity, sweet, and stinky. A reader can imagine smelling these details.
These are words like fuzzy, wet, and soft. A reader can imagine feeling these details.

contents.text: When you write, you can use sensory details. These sense words help your reader understand what something looks, sounds, tastes, smells, or feels like.

table.text: These are words like bright, clean, and purple. A reader can imagine looking at these details.
These are words like hissing, buzzing, and ringing. A reader can imagine hearing these details.
These are words like juicy, sweet, and burnt. A reader can imagine tasting these details.
These are words like fruity, sweet, and stinky. A reader can imagine smelling these details.
These are words like fuzzy, wet, and soft. A reader can imagine feeling these details.

contents.text: Many sense words can describe more than one sense. For example, soft can describe a touch or a sound. And sweet can describe a taste or a smell.
